title: Pentagon Gives Industry 21 Days to Accelerate Production, Army Opens Test Ranges, Egypt Eyes Mecca Pact
subhead: Deputy Defense Secretary Feinberg demands dramatic speedup from defense firms as interceptor stocks run low, the Army opens five test ranges to private companies, and Turkey says Egypt could join the Saudi-Pakistan-Turkey defense pact.

sections.heading: Pentagon to Industry: 21 Days to Show Faster Delivery
sections.body:
Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg sent a memo to major defense companies on Wednesday giving them no more than 21 days to submit plans to 'drive significantly faster, more aggressive delivery schedules and/or increased production for critical capabilities,' according to the document obtained by The Washington Post. 'Years-long development cycles are not acceptable,' Feinberg wrote. 'We must dramatically accelerate our program schedules and expand our production capacity now.'

The directive comes as a CSIS analysis found that the US military has used up close to 80% of its THAAD interceptor inventory and approximately 50% of its Patriot interceptors during the five-month war with Iran. CNN first reported those figures on August 4. The CSIS report warns that depleted inventories may force the US and its Middle Eastern allies to launch fewer interceptors against incoming threats, raising the probability of leakers getting through.

President Trump has pushed back on shortage reports, posting on Truth Social Thursday that the US has 'massive amounts' of munitions and that 'large amounts are being manufactured and shipped.' He has also threatened jail time for officials who share information about military reserves, according to TIME. Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell confirmed the acceleration effort Saturday but insisted it was part of a broader modernization push that predated the Iran conflict.

CNAS senior fellow Stacie Pettyjohn told TIME the DoD is also pursuing a parallel track: cheaper, 'good enough' munitions that can be produced at scale, as reflected in the Defense Innovation Unit's G-BAM (Ground-Based Affordable Mass) Challenge launched in July, which acknowledges that 'current inventories alone' cannot support future conflicts.
sections.whyItMatters: The Feinberg memo is the most explicit official acknowledgment yet that the Iran war is straining US munitions beyond what existing production lines can sustain — and that the acquisition system itself is now seen as a bottleneck, not just factory capacity.

sections.heading: Army Opens Five Test Ranges to Private Industry
sections.body:
Army Secretary Dan Driscoll announced Friday that the Army is opening five military test ranges to private weapons developers, with a goal of cutting the 12-18 month wait time for testing new systems down to 30 days from request. The domestic ranges are at Camp Grayling (Michigan), Camp Shelby (Mississippi), Dugway Proving Ground (Utah), and an unused range at Yuma Proving Ground (Arizona). An overseas site at the Multidomain Training Area in Morocco is also part of the program.

Driscoll said a new online portal and 'concierge' system will allow companies — even those without existing government contracts — to book range access within 30 days. Covenant Industries was the first company through the new system, testing its Anthem missile in Morocco on Thursday, with executive Abby Denburg saying production-ready assets would begin delivery in early 2027.

CSIS senior adviser Mark Cancian described the move as a 'natural step' toward addressing the production pipeline bottleneck, though he noted it addresses testing speed, not manufacturing speed. Driscoll cited Ukraine's rapid defense innovation ecosystem as inspiration: 'If you look at what Ukraine has done so incredibly well, it's this innovation through necessity, and it's innovation at the speed that is near or close to matching the commercial sector.'
sections.whyItMatters: Opening test ranges to non-contracted companies is a meaningful procedural shift — it removes one of the least-visible bottlenecks in the acquisition pipeline. But it only accelerates testing, not production, and the real constraint remains industrial capacity for high-end systems like Patriot and THAAD interceptors that take years to build.

sections.heading: Egypt Could Join the Mecca Defense Pact as Turkey Signals Expansion
sections.body:
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said Saturday that Egypt could join the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement signed Friday between Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan. Fidan told state-run Anadolu Agency the pact 'will not remain limited' to three members and would grow over time to 'bring all countries under this umbrella,' though he only named Egypt specifically. The agreement was signed in Mecca by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif.

Fidan described the mutual defense clause as 'technically the same' as NATO's Article 5 — an attack on one would be considered an attack on all — and insisted the pact was not aimed at Iran or any other country. 'Any country that does not attack us is not a target for us,' he said. The mechanism would require a formal request from the affected member, with assistance ranging from intelligence sharing and logistics to deployment of military units.

Iran has reacted with concern. Iranian parliament member Ebrahim Rezaei said on X that 'a paper agreement with Turkey and Pakistan does not bring security' for Saudi Arabia, comparing it to years of 'unilateral milking of the Americans.' Saudi security analyst Hesham Alghannam told AFP that if proxy attacks on Saudi territory continue, 'I would expect Pakistan to deepen its air defence and advisory role inside the kingdom, and Turkey to accelerate defence-industrial transfers.'

The pact builds on last September's Saudi-Pakistan Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement and covers joint exercises, technology transfer, and intelligence sharing. Pakistan's Defense Minister Khawaja Asif called Israel a 'common threat,' adding a dimension beyond Iran.
sections.whyItMatters: The Mecca Pact is evolving faster than expected. Egypt's potential accession would bring the Arab world's largest military into a framework that already includes NATO's second-largest army, a nuclear power, and the world's largest oil exporter. The technology-transfer clauses matter more than the mutual defense language — they could deepen Turkey-Pakistan defense industrial pipelines in ways that reshape regional arms flows.

sections.heading: Pakistan's China-Backed Western Build-Up Concentrates on India's Flank
sections.body:
Pakistan has advanced three overlapping military programs along its western seaboard in the same weeks it signed the Mecca Pact. According to Firstpost, nearly 250 Chinese SH-15 howitzers have been positioned facing India, a Chinese-built Hangor-class submarine (with AIP technology) has sailed from Karachi, and a new coastal air defense system called Project Ababeel is now operational at Sir Creek, coordinated with the Army's newly formed Rocket Force — modeled on China's PLA Rocket Force.

China sits at the center of every one of these programs. The SH-15 is now produced under licence at Heavy Industries Taxila. The Hangor runs on Chinese AIP technology alongside newly inducted Chinese Tughril-class frigates. Project Ababeel draws on Chinese hovercraft and Turkish drones. The Firstpost analysis notes that 'a rocket force, a coastal air defence system, a submarine and an artillery fleet, all active in the same theatre within the same stretch of months' amounts to more than coincidence — Islamabad appears to be locking in political cover and future technology access for a military posture it is already assembling.
sections.whyItMatters: Pakistan's integrated build-up — with Chinese hardware at every layer and now a trilateral defense pact providing diplomatic cover — represents a qualitative shift from incremental procurement to integrated theatre posture. India's theatre command reform, nearing Cabinet approval, is designed for exactly this kind of layered pressure across a single front.

sections.heading: India Tests Kusha Long-Range SAM as Sudarshan Chakra Takes Shape
sections.body:
India conducted the first flight test of its Kusha long-range surface-to-air missile on July 23, a system developed by the state-run Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO). According to the South China Morning Post, the Kusha is expected to become a key component of Mission Sudarshan Chakra, Prime Minister Modi's plan for a multilayered national air defense umbrella by 2035 against ballistic missiles, fighter aircraft, drones, and other threats.

The test puts a spotlight on India's reliance on imported air defenses — primarily Russia's S-400 Triumf, whose deliveries have been delayed by Moscow's war needs in Ukraine. The Indian Air Force has praised the S-400's performance during Operation Sindoor, claiming it intercepted five Pakistani fighter jets and an early warning aircraft. Retired Air Marshal Ravi Gopal Krishna Kapoor said the Kusha's domestic origin would make it easier to integrate into India's air defense architecture.

Meanwhile, an opinion piece by retired Air Marshal Anil Chopra published by RT on August 8 argued that despite billions in US defense contracts, Washington has yet to satisfy India's demand for meaningful technology transfer, pointing to prolonged GE F414 engine negotiations and F404 delivery delays for the LCA Mk1A as evidence that the relationship remains transactional rather than collaborative.
sections.whyItMatters: India is betting on domestic systems like the Kusha to reduce dependence on imports, but the S-400's combat performance during Operation Sindoor underscores the gap between aspiration and capability. The technology-transfer debate with the US is not new, but it is sharpening as India's Atmanirbhar Bharat doctrine demands more from partners than just platforms.

sections.heading: Nagasaki 81st Anniversary: Nuclear Disarmament at Its Weakest
sections.body:
Nagasaki Mayor Shiro Suzuki delivered the city's Peace Declaration on August 9, marking 81 years since the 1945 atomic bombing. Suzuki noted that more than 12,000 nuclear warheads currently exist on Earth and that three consecutive NPT Review Conferences have failed to adopt a final document toward disarmament. He called nuclear deterrence 'extremely dangerous and fragile' and urged nuclear states to fulfill their NPT obligations.

The declaration also called on the Japanese government to attend the first Review Conference of the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons, scheduled for later this year, and to adopt a security policy that does not rely on nuclear weapons — including realization of a Northeast Asia Nuclear-Weapon-Free Zone. Reuters reported that Japan's leaders are pushing for a renewed debate on nuclear weapons that is unnerving proponents of the country's pacifist constitution.
sections.whyItMatters: The Nagasaki declaration's direct challenge to nuclear deterrence doctrine comes as Japan's own government is moving in the opposite direction — toward discussing nuclear sharing and expanded deterrence. Three failed NPT review conferences and accelerating modernization programs in all nuclear states underscore how far the disarmament framework has deteriorated.

sections.heading: US Navy Announces 'Pivotal Shift' Toward Nearly 20 Guided-Missile Submarines
sections.body:
The US Navy announced this week what analysts call a 'pivotal shift' in its future submarine force: a plan for nearly 20 guided-missile submarines, according to a report highlighted in search results. The move is designed to bolster undersea strike capacity in the Indo-Pacific, where current Virginia-class boats with vertical launch tubes are the only submarines carrying large numbers of land-attack missiles since the retirement of the Ohio-class SSGNs.

The planned expansion of guided-missile submarine capacity is seen as a direct response to the need for greater long-range firepower in a potential Taiwan contingency, where massed missile strikes from survivable platforms would be critical in the opening days of a conflict.
sections.whyItMatters: Submarine-launched cruise missiles are among the most survivable strike options the US has in the Western Pacific. Building toward 20 guided-missile boats would significantly expand the Navy's magazine depth — exactly the kind of capacity concern the Feinberg memo addresses above the waterline.

bottomLine: The Pentagon's 21-day ultimatum to defense firms and the Army's decision to throw open test ranges to private companies are the day's most consequential defense-industry moves — together they represent an admission that the US acquisition system itself, not just factory floors, is a warfighting bottleneck. Meanwhile, the Mecca Pact is already expanding before the ink dries, with Egypt potentially joining a Saudi-Turkey-Pakistan framework that includes NATO-Article-5-style mutual defense and — more consequentially — technology transfer clauses. Pakistan's simultaneous China-backed build-up along Sir Creek and India's Kusha SAM test show the subcontinent's arms dynamics accelerating on both sides. At 81 years since Nagasaki, the nuclear disarmament framework has arguably never looked weaker.
sources: AP, TIME, Washington Post, CNN, CSIS, CNAS, Reuters, Anadolu Agency, Firstpost, South China Morning Post, India TV News, The Media Line, Weekly Blitz, Mainichi Shimbun
